subject: Financial Accounting
title: Government Accounting
outline: Meaning, objectives and characteristics of government accounting
Bases of accounting: cash, accrual and commitment
Sources of government revenue at federal, state and local levels
Capital and recurrent expenditure; the Consolidated Revenue Fund
The budget, warrants and the appropriation process
Officers and instruments of public sector financial control
Comparison between public sector and private sector accounting

modules.title: Nature, Objectives and Bases of Government Accounting
modules.html:
1. Meaning

Government accounting is the process of recording, analysing, classifying, summarising, communicating and interpreting financial information about government in aggregate and in detail, reflecting all transactions involving the receipt, transfer and disposition of public funds and property.

2. Objectives

  1. To demonstrate the legality of transactions and their conformity with the Appropriation Act.
  2. To provide evidence of accountability and stewardship for public funds.
  3. To disclose the results of the custody and management of public money.
  4. To provide information for planning, budgeting and control.
  5. To help evaluate the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of government programmes.

3. Bases of Accounting

BasisRecognition ruleComment
Cash basisRevenue when received, expenditure when paidSimple, objective; the traditional Nigerian public sector basis
Accrual basisRevenue when earned, expenditure when incurredShows assets and liabilities; adopted under IPSAS accrual
Commitment basisExpenditure recognised when an order is placedGuards against over-spending a vote
Modified cash / modified accrualCash basis extended for a short period after year end, or accrual excluding fixed assetsPractical compromises

Nigeria has adopted IPSAS (International Public Sector Accounting Standards), moving from cash basis to accrual basis reporting.

4. Distinctive Characteristics

  • Emphasis on legal compliance rather than profit measurement.
  • Use of fund accounting - money is kept in distinct funds for specified purposes.
  • Budget is a legal authority, not merely a plan.
  • Fixed assets historically expensed rather than capitalised under the cash basis.

examples.q: State three differences between public sector and private sector accounting.
examples.a: (i) Objective: government accounting aims at accountability and legal compliance, while private sector accounting aims at measuring profit and financial position. (ii) Basis: the public sector traditionally uses the cash (now moving to IPSAS accrual) basis whereas businesses use the accrual basis throughout. (iii) Ownership and regulation: government funds belong to the public and are regulated by the Constitution, the Finance (Control and Management) Act and the Appropriation Act, while companies are governed by CAMA and IFRS. Others: government uses fund accounting and a legally binding budget, and prepares no profit and loss account or dividend.

examples.q: Explain the commitment basis and give one advantage and one disadvantage.
examples.a: Under the commitment basis, expenditure is recorded as soon as a local purchase order or contract commits the government, before payment is made. Advantage: it prevents a ministry from exceeding its vote because unpaid commitments already reduce the available balance. Disadvantage: it can overstate expenditure for the year if commitments are later cancelled, and it requires additional records and adjustments at year end.

modules.title: Revenue, Expenditure and Public Funds
modules.html:
1. Sources of Federal Government Revenue

  • Petroleum profit tax, royalties and crude oil sales.
  • Companies income tax, value added tax, capital gains tax, education tax.
  • Customs and excise duties.
  • Licences, fees, fines, earnings from government enterprises, rents on government property.
  • Internal and external loans, grants and aid.

2. State and Local Government Revenue

State: statutory allocation from the Federation Account, personal income tax (PAYE), pools betting and gaming taxes, road taxes, stamp duties on individuals, internally generated revenue, and grants.
Local government: statutory allocation, tenement rates, shop and kiosk rates, market and motor park levies, birth/death and marriage registration fees, radio and television licences, and bicycle/cart permits.

3. Classification of Expenditure

Recurrent expenditureCapital expenditure
Salaries, wages and allowancesConstruction of roads, bridges, schools
Pensions and gratuitiesPurchase of vehicles, plant and machinery
Maintenance, utilities, stationeryAcquisition of land and buildings
Debt servicing (interest)Repayment of loan principal, equity investment

4. Public Funds

  • Consolidated Revenue Fund (CRF) - the main fund into which all federal revenue is paid; withdrawals require appropriation by the National Assembly.
  • Development (Capital) Fund - finances capital projects.
  • Contingencies Fund - meets urgent and unforeseen expenditure.
  • Federation Account - shared among the three tiers of government under an approved revenue allocation formula.

5. Budget and Financial Control

The budget passes through preparation by ministries, consolidation by the Budget Office, presentation by the President, debate and passage as the Appropriation Act, then execution and reporting. Spending is released through warrants (Annual General Warrant, Provisional General Warrant, Supplementary Warrant, Reserve Expenditure Warrant, Virement Warrant).

Officers and instruments: the Accountant-General of the Federation (custodian of accounts and treasury), the Auditor-General for the Federation (independent audit and report to the Public Accounts Committee), the Minister of Finance, Accounting Officers (Permanent Secretaries), the Financial Regulations, Treasury and Finance Circulars, the Public Accounts Committee, and the Fiscal Responsibility Act. A vote book records commitments and payments against each budget head and subhead to prevent over-expenditure.

examples.q: Classify the following as capital or recurrent expenditure: (i) salaries of teachers; (ii) construction of a bridge; (iii) purchase of textbooks for a ministry library; (iv) interest on a foreign loan; (v) repayment of the principal of a loan.
examples.a: (i) Recurrent - regular operating cost. (ii) Capital - creates a long-lasting asset. (iii) Recurrent - consumable running cost (unless part of a capital project). (iv) Recurrent - debt servicing is a running cost. (v) Capital - repayment of principal reduces liability and is charged to the capital/development fund.

examples.q: What is the Consolidated Revenue Fund and how may money be withdrawn from it?
examples.a: The Consolidated Revenue Fund is the principal fund of the Federal Government into which all revenues and receipts are paid, except those payable into another fund established by law. No money may be withdrawn from it except to meet expenditure charged upon the fund by the Constitution (e.g. the salaries of judges and the Auditor-General) or where the withdrawal has been authorised by an Appropriation Act, a Supplementary Appropriation Act, or a law passed by the National Assembly, and the withdrawal must be made in the manner prescribed by the National Assembly.

modules.title: Bases of accounting: cash, accrual and commitment
modules.html:
Bases of accounting: cash, accrual and commitment is a key part of Government Accounting (SSS 3, Financial Accounting). Master the meaning, the main points and how it is tested in JAMB and WAEC questions on this topic.

Key points

  • Meaning Government accounting is the process of recording, analysing, classifying, summarising, communicating and interpreting financial information about government in aggregate and in detail, reflecting all transactions involving the receipt, transfer and disposition of public funds and property.
  • Bases of Accounting Basis Recognition rule Comment Cash basis Revenue when received, expenditure when paid Simple, objective; the traditional Nigerian public sector basis Accrual basis Revenue when earned, expenditure when incurred Shows assets and liabilities; adopted under IPSAS accrual Commitment basis Expenditure recognised when an order is placed Guards against over-spending a vote Modified cash / modified accrual Cash basis extended for a short period after year end, or accrual excluding fixed assets Practical compromises Nigeria has adopted IPSAS (International Public Sector Accounting Standards), moving from cash basis to accrual basis reporting.
  • Use of fund accounting - money is kept in distinct funds for specified purposes.
  • Fixed assets historically expensed rather than capitalised under the cash basis.
  • Officers and instruments: the Accountant-General of the Federation (custodian of accounts and treasury), the Auditor-General for the Federation (independent audit and report to the Public Accounts Committee), the Minister of Finance, Accounting Officers (Permanent Secretaries), the Financial Regulations, Treasury and Finance Circulars, the Public Accounts Committee, and the Fiscal Responsibility Act.

Worked example

Q: Government accounting is chiefly concerned with:
A: Accountability for public funds — Public sector accounting emphasises stewardship, legality and accountability rather than profit.

Q: Under the cash basis, revenue is recognised when:
A: Received — The cash basis records revenue only on actual receipt and expenditure only on payment.

examples.q: Government accounting is chiefly concerned with:
examples.a: Accountability for public funds — Public sector accounting emphasises stewardship, legality and accountability rather than profit.

examples.q: Under the cash basis, revenue is recognised when:
examples.a: Received — The cash basis records revenue only on actual receipt and expenditure only on payment.

modules.title: The budget, warrants and the appropriation process
modules.html:
The budget, warrants and the appropriation process is a key part of Government Accounting (SSS 3, Financial Accounting). Master the meaning, the main points and how it is tested in JAMB and WAEC questions on this topic.

Key points

  • Meaning Government accounting is the process of recording, analysing, classifying, summarising, communicating and interpreting financial information about government in aggregate and in detail, reflecting all transactions involving the receipt, transfer and disposition of public funds and property.
  • Objectives To demonstrate the legality of transactions and their conformity with the Appropriation Act.
  • To provide information for planning, budgeting and control.
  • Budget is a legal authority, not merely a plan.
  • Public Funds Consolidated Revenue Fund (CRF) - the main fund into which all federal revenue is paid; withdrawals require appropriation by the National Assembly.

Worked example

Q: Money for urgent and unforeseen expenditure is drawn from the:
A: Contingencies Fund — The Contingencies Fund exists for urgent, unforeseen needs pending supplementary appropriation.

Q: The Appropriation Act:
A: Authorises expenditure from public funds — It is the legal authority for spending the amounts contained in the budget.

examples.q: Money for urgent and unforeseen expenditure is drawn from the:
examples.a: Contingencies Fund — The Contingencies Fund exists for urgent, unforeseen needs pending supplementary appropriation.
Authorises expenditure from public funds — It is the legal authority for spending the amounts contained in the budget.

quiz.q: Government accounting is chiefly concerned with:
quiz.solution: Public sector accounting emphasises stewardship, legality and accountability rather than profit.

quiz.q: Under the cash basis, revenue is recognised when:
quiz.solution: The cash basis records revenue only on actual receipt and expenditure only on payment.

quiz.q: The basis that records expenditure once a purchase order is issued is the:
quiz.solution: Commitment accounting charges the vote as soon as the government is committed, preventing over-spending.

quiz.q: Which is a source of local government revenue?
quiz.solution: Tenement rates on property are a classic local government levy; the others are federal taxes.

quiz.q: The fund into which all federal revenue is paid is the:
quiz.solution: The Consolidated Revenue Fund is the main receptacle for federal receipts.

quiz.q: Money for urgent and unforeseen expenditure is drawn from the:
quiz.solution: The Contingencies Fund exists for urgent, unforeseen needs pending supplementary appropriation.

quiz.q: Construction of a new hospital is:
quiz.solution: It creates a long-lived asset and is charged to capital.

quiz.q: The officer responsible for auditing government accounts is the:
quiz.solution: The Auditor-General independently audits public accounts and reports to the National Assembly.

quiz.q: The Appropriation Act:
quiz.solution: It is the legal authority for spending the amounts contained in the budget.

quiz.q: A virement warrant permits:
options: Transfer of funds from one subhead to another
quiz.solution: Virement reallocates approved funds between subheads without increasing the total vote.

quiz.q: Companies income tax is collected by:
quiz.solution: FIRS collects federal taxes such as companies income tax, VAT and petroleum profit tax.

quiz.q: Personal income tax of individuals resident in a state is collected by:
options: The State Board of Internal Revenue
quiz.solution: PAYE and other personal income taxes of residents accrue to the state government (except armed forces, police and FCT residents).

quiz.q: Government accounting differs from commercial accounting because it uses:
quiz.solution: Public funds are segregated into distinct funds for specified purposes; double entry and ledgers are used by both.

quiz.q: The vote book is maintained to:
options: Control expenditure against approved budget heads
quiz.solution: It shows the amount voted, commitments made and payments, so that no head is over-spent.

quiz.q: IPSAS stands for:
quiz.solution: IPSAS are the standards adopted by Nigerian governments for public sector financial reporting.

quiz.q: Which of these is charged directly on the Consolidated Revenue Fund without annual appropriation?
quiz.solution: Constitutionally protected salaries, such as those of the Auditor-General and judicial officers, are statutory charges on the CRF.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a source of revenue for the government?
quiz.solution: Taxes (CIT, PIT, VAT, etc.) are the primary means by which a government generates income to fund public expenditure.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a source of government revenue?
quiz.solution: Taxes (CIT, VAT, etc.) are the primary means through which the government generates revenue for public expenditure.

quiz.q: Which of the following describes 'Consolidated Revenue Fund'?
options: A fund where all government revenues are paid
quiz.solution: In Nigerian public finance, all revenues received by the Federation (unless otherwise directed) must be paid into the CRF.

quiz.q: The Consolidated Revenue Fund (CRF) is?
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: Government's main account.

quiz.q: In a limited liability company, the part of authorized capital that has been offered to the public for subscription is _____.
quiz.solution: Issued capital is the portion of authorized (nominal) capital that the company has actually sent out for investors to buy.

quiz.q: In a limited liability company, the part of authorized capital that has been taken up by the public is _____.
quiz.solution: Issued capital is the portion of authorized capital that the directors have decided to offer to the public for subscription.

quiz.q: Revenue Expenditure is charged to:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2021). Correct answer: P & L Account.

quiz.q: Consolidated Fund is associated with:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2021). Correct answer: Public Sector.

quiz.q: Revenue Expenditure:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2023). Correct answer: Day to day expenses.

quiz.q: Public Sector Acc:
quiz.solution: Past question (NECO 2025). Correct answer: Government.

quiz.q: Consolidated Fund:
quiz.solution: Past question (NECO 2025). Correct answer: Govt Revenue.

quiz.q: Capital Expenditure creates?
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: Fixed Assets.

quiz.q: Revenue Expenditure is for?
quiz.solution: Past-question bank (legacy TXT). Correct answer: Day-to-day running.

quiz.q: What is the correct entry for recording a cash discount allowed to a customer?
options: Debit: Discount Received; Credit: Customer's Account
Debit: Customer's Account; Credit: Discount Allowed
Debit: Discount Allowed; Credit: Customer's Account
quiz.solution: Discount Allowed is an expense. To record it, you debit the expense account (Discount Allowed) and credit the personal account of the customer.

quiz.q: The reward for a partner for providing capital to the firm is _____.
quiz.solution: Interest on capital is an appropriation of profit designed to compensate partners for the amount of capital they have invested in the partnership.

quiz.q: The document showing the financial position of a business at a specific date is the _____.
quiz.solution: The Balance Sheet (Statement of Financial Position) lists assets, liabilities, and capital to show what a business is worth at a specific point in time.

quiz.q: Authorized capital is also known as _____.
quiz.solution: Nominal or registered capital is the maximum amount of share capital a company is legally allowed to issue.

quiz.q: Which of the following describes a 'Capital Reserve'?
options: Profit from the sale of a fixed asset
Money set aside for paying wages
quiz.solution: Capital reserves are created from non-trading activities, such as the profit on sale of non-current assets or revaluation of assets.

quiz.q: Working Capital is defined as _____.
quiz.solution: Working capital measures the short-term liquidity of a business, indicating its ability to pay off debts due within a year.

quiz.q: The process of transferring transactions from the journals to the ledger is known as _____.
quiz.solution: Posting is the technical term for transferring entries from the books of original entry (journals) to the principal book of accounts (the ledger).

quiz.q: The petty cash system where the petty cashier is given a fixed sum at the start of a period is the _____ system.
quiz.solution: In the Imprest system, the petty cashier starts with a float and is reimbursed exactly what was spent at the end of the period.

quiz.q: What is the correct entry for recording a cash purchase of goods?
quiz.solution: Purchases (an expense) increase on the debit side, and Cash (an asset) decreases on the credit side.

quiz.q: Authorized Capital is:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2021). Correct answer: Maximum capital allowed to issue.

quiz.q: Authorized share capital is:
options: Maximum capital a company can issue
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2022). Correct answer: Maximum capital a company can issue.

quiz.q: Working Capital:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2023). Correct answer: $$ CA - CL $$.

quiz.q: Authorized Capital:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2023). Correct answer: Registered maximum.

quiz.q: Three column cash book has:
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2023). Correct answer: Cash, Bank, Discount.

quiz.q: In a partnership, interest on capital is...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: An appropriation of profit.

quiz.q: Revenue is recognized as soon as goods are sold or services are rendered. This is based on...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: Realization concept.

quiz.q: The petty cash system where the petty cashier is given a fixed sum at the beginning of a period is...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: Imprest system.

quiz.q: Working Capital is calculated as...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: Current Assets - Current Liabilities.

quiz.q: The document issued by a company to invite the public to subscribe for shares is the...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: Prospectus.

quiz.q: The capital of a company is divided into small units called...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: Shares.

quiz.q: A statement showing the financial position of a business at a particular date is the...
quiz.solution: Past question (JAMB 2024). Correct answer: Balance Sheet.
